messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a fifty-eight-year-old hairdresser who runs a small shop in a busy neighborhood, married for thirty-two years. Nine months ago he was closing up late on a Thursday evening. A man emerged from the alley beside the shop, reeking of cheap whiskey, and demanded his cash. When Kwame hesitated the man shoved him against the wall and snarled, “You think you’re better than me? Look at you, shaking like a child.” Kwame handed over the day’s earnings. The man shoved him again, spat at his feet, and disappeared. Kwame stood frozen for a long moment, then locked the door and drove home in silence.

The first pictures came that night. In his mind the image of the man’s face—pocked skin, bloodshot eyes—stuck like a photograph he could not look away from. Within days the memory had become a film: the smell of whiskey, the feel of the wall against his back, the insult, all of it playing over and over, sometimes in the middle of a haircut. When his wife asked what happened he found he could not answer. He knew the facts, but the words would not come—the event seemed to live somewhere beyond language, in sounds and sensations that resisted description.

Now a customer’s criticism—even a gentle correction about a part line or a request for a trim—hits him like the robber’s words did. Just last week a woman said, “The left side is a little longer, can you fix it?” and Kwame’s throat tightened. The alcohol smell on a man waiting for a haircut does the same: the olfactory cue yanks him straight back into that alley, the film starting before he can stop it. When he notices a person lingering outside the shop—not doing anything overt—he is certain they are dangerous, watching him, and the replay begins again.

What frightens Kwame most is that the memory does not simply arrive; it changes him. After a flashback he sits in the back room and goes over everything he might have done wrong. Should he have closed earlier? Should he have fought back? Should he have called the police? He dwells on these questions for hours, picking at his own choices until he feels worthless and ashamed. The shame makes him try even harder to suppress the images, to push them away, but suppression only seems to make the film run more frequently. He has started avoiding people altogether. He no longer takes evening haircuts. He leaves the shop early, walking fast with his head down. When a familiar client sits in his chair he finds himself cutting in silence, unwilling to engage, his hands trembling slightly. His wife notices that he has stopped attending their weekly dinner with friends. He tells her he is tired, but the truth is that being around anyone feels like a threat—one wrong word, one critical glance, and the whole scene will start again.

Avoidance has created a loop he cannot see. Because he avoids social contact, he is never exposed to people who might confirm he is safe. Instead he grows more sensitized: every person who acts suspiciously becomes a sign of danger, and that perception triggers the memory, which triggers more self-blame, which drives him deeper into isolation. Even the salon—once a place of pride—has become a minefield. A client’s offhand complaint sets off the film, and then for the rest of the day he replays the criticism alongside the mugging, as if the two are the same failure.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a morning last month when a man with a whiskey odor walked into the shop. Kwame excused himself, locked himself in the supply closet, and stood shaking until the man left. His wife found him sitting on the floor, unable to explain. She pushed him to call a therapist. Now, sitting in the waiting room, he is terrified that talking about the event will make the film play endlessly. But more than that he is exhausted—tired of the pictures, tired of the silence with his family, tired of a mind that turns every small moment into a reminder of his worst night. He hopes, quietly, that someone can help him stop the film from starting.
